name: TXB0102DCUR
title: TXB0102: 2-bit bidirectional voltage-level translator, automatic direction sensing
summary: Two non-inverting channels that pass logic signals both ways between an A side powered from 1.2 V to 3.6 V and a B side powered from 1.65 V to 5.5 V, with VCCA never above VCCB. There is no direction pin: each I/O is held by a weak driver that an outside driver can overpower, and edge-triggered one-shots speed up each transition. Pulling OE low, or taking either supply to ground, leaves every I/O in high impedance, and Ioff keeps an unpowered part from back-feeding. It is for push-pull CMOS signals only, not open-drain buses.
key_figures: 100 Mbps (VCCA 2.5 V or 3.3 V); 60 Mbps at 1.8 V; 40 Mbps at 1.5 V; 20 Mbps at 1.2 V
A port ±2500 V; B port ±1500 V (JS-001)

notes: Body size, nominal: DCU (VSSOP-8) 2.30 mm × 2.00 mm; YZP (DSBGA-8) 0.90 mm × 1.80 mm.

circuits.title: Typical operating circuit
circuits.description: A controller on a 1.8 V rail talks to a system on a 3.3 V rail over two data lines. The 1.8 V rail feeds VCCA and the 3.3 V rail feeds VCCB, each with a 0.1 µF capacitor to ground. A1 and A2 go to the controller's data pins, B1 and B2 to the system's; the part works out the direction on its own. The controller drives OE, and a resistor from OE to ground keeps the I/Os in high impedance while the supplies come up.

parts.note: OE pulldown; its least value is set by how much current the OE driver can source.

notes: VCCA ≤ VCCB.
Pullup or pulldown resistors on the data lines, if any, are above 50 kΩ.

equations.name: Input current peaks while the I/O is held against the opposite level
equations.expr: IIN(peak) = VT / 4 kΩ (just below VT); IIN(peak) = –(VD – VT) / 4 kΩ (just above VT)

where.VT: input threshold of the part, typically VCCI/2

equations.note: Typical IIN against VIN: IIN climbs linearly from zero to VT / 4 kΩ as VIN rises to VT, steps to –(VD – VT) / 4 kΩ, then climbs back toward zero as VIN rises further.

operation.text: No direction signal is needed. Each I/O pair has a buffer each way through a 4 kΩ series resistor, so at DC the outputs hold their level only weakly and a driver on either side can take over the line. One-shots watch for edges on both ports: on a rising edge they briefly switch on PMOS transistors to pull the line up fast, on a falling edge NMOS transistors to pull it down. During a transition the output impedance is typically 70 Ω for VCCO of 1.2 V to 1.8 V, 50 Ω for 1.8 V to 3.3 V, and 40 Ω for 3.3 V to 5 V.

Whatever drives a data I/O needs at least ±2 mA of drive. Holding the line against the part's weak output, the input current grows with VIN to a peak of VT / 4 kΩ just below the threshold, then reverses to –(VD – VT) / 4 kΩ just above it and shrinks again, VT being about VCCI/2 and VD the outside driver's supply.

Each one-shot stays on for about 10 ns. Traces are kept short enough that a reflection returns within that time, while the driver is still low impedance. Heavy capacitance can outlast the one-shot before the line reaches the rail; trace and connector capacitance add to the lumped load, and too much brings retriggering, contention or ringing. The outputs drive up to 70 pF.

OE low puts every I/O in high impedance; OE high enables the part. These are its only two modes. tdis is the delay from OE falling to the outputs going high impedance; ten is the time after OE rises before the one-shots are working. OE is powered from VCCA.

Resistors on the I/Os are not recommended. Where one is needed it is above 50 kΩ so it does not fight the weak output drivers; a smaller value drags VOH down or VOL up (equations). For the same reason the part does not suit open-drain buses such as I2C or 1-Wire; the TXS01xx translators serve those.

In operation VCCA stays at or below VCCB. During power-up either supply may come up first; VCCA above VCCB then does no harm. With either supply at 0 V all outputs are disabled. To keep the I/Os in high impedance through power-up and power-down, OE is tied to ground through a pulldown and not driven high until both supplies are up and steady; the pulldown's smallest value depends on how much current the OE driver can source.
Ioff circuitry turns the outputs off when the part is unpowered, so no current flows back into it.

Bypass capacitors sit right at the VCCA, VCCB and GND pins; the typical layout uses 0.1 µF on each supply. Signal traces are short, keeping the round-trip delay of a reflection under the roughly 10 ns one-shot time. OE is held low until both supplies are up.
